dialog.body: Zoning and Inspections, this is Anita. How can I help you?
Hi, yes, hello. I hope I've got the right office. I'm trying to find out about putting up a fence? Or, well, whether I'm allowed to.
You've got the right place. Let's start with where it would go. What's the address?

It's 345 Gidley Street. In the Fifth Ward, I think they call it. It's my shop, actually, I own the building, and the side of it runs along a really busy road, so there's all this noise and, I don't know, dust and people cutting through.
Okay, so a fence along the side by the road. What kind of fence are you thinking about?

A stockade fence. You know, the kind with the pointed tops, the boards close together. I was thinking cedar. And about four and a half feet tall. Is that, um, is that a normal height? I honestly don't know what's normal.
Four and a half feet is within what people commonly put up, yes. Is it solid boards, no gaps?

Solid, yeah. Oh, hang on, one second. [pause] I dropped my reading glasses. They're somewhere on the floor, I'm feeling around by my feet here. I had a whole list written down and I can't read my own handwriting without them. [pause] Oh, I'm sorry, what was I saying?
No worries, take your time. You were telling me it's a solid cedar stockade fence, about four and a half feet.

Right, right. So my main question is, do I need a permit for that? Or paperwork of any kind? Because my cousin said you don't for a little fence, but then my neighbor said you do for everything, and now I'm just, I don't know who to believe.

Understandable, you've heard two answers. In general, a fence often does need a permit here, and it can depend on the height and where on the property it sits. Since yours is next to a road, location matters too. So I'd plan on filing something before you hire anyone or buy materials.
Oh. So it's a yes. Or a maybe yes? Is there a height where you don't need one? Is that what my cousin meant?

Could be. Some places have a height cutoff, but I don't want you relying on a number from me over the phone. The safe move is to apply, and the application will tell you if it's something that's waived. Do you own the property or lease it?
I own it. Own the building and the lot. Well, the bank owns some of it, ha, but I mean it's mine.
Good, that makes it simpler. Then you'd be the applicant.

Okay. And the other thing, how close to the property line can I put it? Because I wanted it right up against the edge so I don't lose any of the parking, but I'm not sure that's allowed. Or is it supposed to be back a few feet? Is it a foot? Two feet?

That's one of the things we check. Sometimes a fence can sit right on or near the line, and sometimes there's a setback, especially near a road or at a corner where drivers need to see. Do you know if your lot is on a corner?
Um, kind of? The road is on the side. So yes, I guess it's a corner. Is that bad?

Not bad, it just means the visibility at the corner gets looked at. It would help to have a survey or a plot plan showing where your line is, so you're not guessing. Do you have one from when you bought?
I think so. Somewhere in a folder. Oh, found them! The glasses, I mean. They were under the chair. Okay, now I can see my list. Ha. Where was I?
You were asking about the line. So, to sum up: bring or send the plot plan, a simple sketch of the fence with the length and height, and say it's cedar. The application will sort out the setback.
Okay, plot plan, sketch, length, height, cedar. Wait, do I send it here or is it online? I'm not sure I'm following which office does what.
You can bring it to the zoning counter at City Hall, and I can also take your number in case someone needs to call you back. Is the number you're on a good one?
Got it, 401-555-0175. I'll note that you're asking about a four-and-a-half-foot cedar stockade at 345 Gidley.
That's it. Okay. I think I've got it, mostly. Permit probably, plot plan, and they'll tell me about the line. Thank you so much, and sorry about the glasses circus.
No trouble at all. Have a good afternoon.
You too, bye now.
